Kana. The two phonetic scripts of Japanese—hiragana and katakana—derived from Chinese characters but designed for phonetic representation rather than pictographic meaning. Developed around the ninth century, kana enabled the vernacular written expression that had previously been restricted to classical Chinese, democratizing literacy and allowing women authors in particular to forge a literary tradition.

The two scripts serve different purposes. Hiragana is used for native Japanese words and grammatical particles, while katakana was originally reserved for Buddhist priestly annotations but is now used for foreign words and emphasis. Chinese characters, kanji, encode meaning but are phonetically ambiguous in Japanese. Kana solved this problem by providing a fixed sound per symbol, making reading and writing far more accessible to ordinary people.

Hiragana characters are curved and flowing, derived by simplifying kanji radicals, while katakana characters are angular and geometric, derived from kanji components in a different way. Their visual distinction carries semantic weight. Women of the Heian court, including Murasaki Shikibu and Sei Shonagon, gained unprecedented literary voice precisely because they were allowed to write in kana while men were obligated to use the prestige language of Chinese.

The Tale of Genji and The Pillow Book, cornerstone works of world literature, were written in kana by women who would have been denied access to classical scholarly training in Chinese and its literature. The development of kana was not instantaneous but evolved gradually during the eighth and ninth centuries as scribes developed shorthand systems. By the Heian period, both scripts had standardized forms.
